why_how.text: A parked car that sits in a travel lane or out of sight becomes a hazard for every driver who comes along.
Setting the brake and the right gear every time keeps a parked car from rolling.

scenario.text: Maria parks her automatic car at the curb and plans to run into a shop for a few minutes.

reasoning.text: She sets the parking brake, leaves the car in park, takes the keys and locks it because it will be out of her sight.

result.text: Her car is secured and no key is left inside.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the parking brake is only needed on hills.

correction.text: The guide says to set the parking brake every time you park, along with gear for a manual or park for an automatic.

memory_support.text: Brake on, gear or park, keys out, doors locked.

prompt.text: You drive a manual car and park on a flat street. How do you leave the transmission, and what else do you set?

answer.text: Leave it in gear and set the parking brake.

rationale.text: A manual stays in gear and an automatic stays in park, and the parking brake is set in both cases.

lines.text: How to secure it every time.

narration.text: Welcome to the parking chapter. Parking sounds simple, but a car left in the wrong place or left unsecured can become a hazard for everyone who passes it. In this first lesson you will learn where a parked car belongs, why a designated parking area is the first choice, and what to do if you have to stop on the roadway itself. Then you will learn the routine that secures a car every single time you park: the parking brake, the right gear for a manual or an automatic, the keys and the locks. These habits carry through every other lesson in this chapter.

title.text: Clear of lanes, easy to see

lines.text: Leave the car clear of travel lanes.
Drivers from both directions should see it.
Use a designated area when you can.

narration.text: Once your car is parked, it must not turn into a hazard. That means leaving it far enough from any travel lane that it does not get in the way, and in a place where drivers coming from either direction can see it. The guide also says to use a designated parking area whenever you can, because those spaces are built to keep parked cars out of traffic. The general test is simple: never park where your vehicle blocks normal traffic or creates a hazard for other drivers. If a spot would force others to swerve or would hide your car, it is the wrong spot.

lines.text: Get as far from traffic as you can.
Pull close to the curb if there is one.

narration.text: Sometimes there is no lot or marked space and you have to park on the roadway itself. When that happens, the guide gives two clear instructions. First, get as far away from moving traffic as you can, so passing cars have as much room as possible. Second, if there is a curb, pull as close to it as possible. A car left a few feet out from the curb narrows the lane and invites a crash. Combined with the hazard rule from the last slide, this means a roadway stop should leave the car tucked tight to the edge, visible, and clear of the lane.

lines.text: Set the parking brake every time.

narration.text: Every time you park, two things happen before you leave the car. You set the parking brake, and you put the transmission in its parked position. For a manual transmission that means leaving it in gear. For an automatic it means leaving it in park. The brake and the gear work together, so a car on even a slight slope stays where you left it. This is not a hill-only rule. The guide says every time you park, on any street, in any weather. Make it automatic, the same way buckling your seat belt is automatic when you get in.

Here is the trap. Many new drivers know that a car should be left in some gear, but they mix up which car gets which setting. The rule splits by transmission type. A manual car is left in gear, because a manual has no park position. An automatic car is left in park. In both cases the parking brake is set as well. Neutral is never the parked position for either one. If a question describes a manual car left in park or an automatic left in gear, the answer has the two settings reversed. Remember the pair: manual in gear, automatic in park, brake on for both.

Here is a quick check: you drive a manual car and park on a flat street outside a friend's house. How do you leave the transmission, and what else do you set before you walk away? Work it out before reading on. The answer is that a manual car is left in gear, and the parking brake is set. If you said park, remember that park is the setting for an automatic. And if you thought the brake only matters on hills, the guide says to set it every time you park. Finally, take your keys with you and lock the car, since it will be out of your sight.

lines.text: Never leave keys in a parked car.
Lock it when it is out of sight.

narration.text: To finish, the last part of every parking routine is security. Never leave the keys in a parked vehicle, even for a short errand, and lock the car any time it will be out of your sight. So the full habit is: choose a designated area when you can, keep the car clear of travel lanes and easy to see, pull close to the curb if you must use the roadway, set the parking brake, leave a manual in gear or an automatic in park, take the keys and lock up. Next you will learn how to get out of the car and pull away safely. Practice it until it feels automatic.

why_how.text: Opening a door into traffic or into a cyclist's path is one of the easiest ways to cause a crash while parked.
Pulling out without checking and signaling surprises the drivers already moving.

scenario.text: Ken parks on a busy street with his young daughter in the back seat on the street side.

reasoning.text: He checks for traffic and cyclists and has his daughter slide over and get out on the curb side.

result.text: They leave the car safely, and Ken closes his door as soon as he is out.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the street-side door can never be used.

correction.text: The street-side door is allowed after you check traffic first; the curb side is simply preferred.

memory_support.text: Look, curb side out, shut fast, then check and signal.

prompt.text: You parked and need to get out on the street side. What must you do first?

answer.text: Check traffic first, and watch for cyclists before opening the door.

rationale.text: The street-side door is allowed only after a traffic check, and cyclists often ride along the right edge beside parked cars.

narration.text: This lesson covers the moments just before and just after a parked car. Getting out of the car and pulling back into traffic are both times when drivers are easy to surprise. You will learn the door routine the guide recommends: look for traffic before any door opens, use the curb side whenever you can, keep children on the curb side, watch for cyclists, and close your door as soon as you are out. Then you will learn the two steps that come before pulling out of any parking space. These are short habits, but they prevent some very common crashes.

lines.text: Look for traffic before opening a door.
Get out on the curb side when possible.
Children leave on the curb side too.

narration.text: Before you open your door, look for traffic. Then, whenever possible, get out on the curb side of the car, away from moving vehicles. The same goes for your passengers, and the guide singles out children: have them leave the car on the curb side too. Children may not judge traffic well, and the curb side keeps them away from the travel lane. If your passenger is sitting behind you on the street side, it is safer for them to slide across the seat and step out onto the curb than to open the street-side door into traffic.

lines.text: Cyclists ride along the right edge.
They pass right beside parked cars.
Close the door once you are out.

narration.text: Cars are not the only traffic to watch for. Before opening a door, look for cyclists. The guide explains why: cyclists often ride along the right edge of the travel lanes, right next to parked cars, so a door swung open without looking can strike a rider who has nowhere to go. After you check and step out, close the door as soon as you are out of the car. An open door left hanging into the lane is a hazard for both cyclists and drivers. Look, open, step out, and close, in that order, every time you leave a parked car.

lines.text: Street side is allowed after a check.

narration.text: Here is a common trap. Some learners think the guide forbids the street-side door entirely, while others think it does not matter which side they use. Neither is right. The guide prefers the curb side, but opening a door on the street side is allowed after you check traffic first. So the rule has two parts that work together: the curb side is the first choice, and the street side is acceptable only after a traffic check. On a test, an answer that says never use the street side, or that says no check is needed, misses one of those two parts.

When you are ready to leave a parking space, the guide gives two steps that apply to every space: check traffic and signal. Checking traffic means looking for cars, cyclists and people around you before the car moves. Signaling tells everyone nearby that you are about to pull out, so they are not surprised by a car suddenly entering the lane. Do both before you move, not after you are already halfway into the street. This applies whether you are leaving a curb, a lot space, or a spot on a hill. Check, signal, then move only when the way is clear.

lines.text: You must exit on the street side.

narration.text: Here is a quick check: you parked along a busy street and, this time, you need to get out on the street side. What must you do before you open the door? Work it out before reading on. The answer is to check traffic first, and that includes watching for cyclists, who often ride along the right edge of the travel lanes right beside parked cars. The street-side door is allowed after that check, though the curb side is preferred whenever it is possible. Once you are out, close the door as soon as you can so it does not hang into the lane.

lines.text: Look, exit curb side, close fast.
Check and signal to pull out.

narration.text: Let us pull this lesson together. Before any door opens, look for traffic and for cyclists along the right edge of the lanes. Get out on the curb side when you can, and have passengers, especially children, do the same. If you must use the street-side door, check traffic first. Close the door as soon as you are out. When you leave the space, check traffic and signal before you move. In the next lesson you will learn the places where parking is not allowed at all, and how street type, signs and colored curbs change where you may stop.

why_how.text: Parking in the wrong place blocks crossings, driveways and emergency equipment, or forces traffic to go around you.
The side of the street you may use depends on whether traffic runs one way or both ways.

scenario.text: Ana finds an open spot on the left side of a two-way street, right beside a yellow curb.

reasoning.text: Left-side parking on a two-way street is not allowed, and a yellow curb means no parking.

result.text: She moves on and finds a legal spot on the right side.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that if no sign is posted, parking must be allowed.

correction.text: Colored curb markings can limit parking even where no sign is posted, and a yellow curb means no parking.

memory_support.text: One-way, either side; two-way, never the left.

prompt.text: You find an empty spot on the left side of a two-way street. May you park there?

answer.text: No. The left side of a two-way street is not allowed.

rationale.text: Only a one-way street usually allows either side; a two-way street forbids the left side and facing against traffic.

lines.text: Street sides that change with traffic.

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn where you may not park. Some of the rules depend on the street: whether traffic flows one way or both ways changes which side you may use. Others depend on what you see: signs and colored curb markings can ban or limit parking. And some places are always off limits, such as intersections, crosswalks, sidewalks, driveway entrances, bridges, yellow curbs and fire hydrants. By the end, you should be able to look at any curb and decide quickly whether parking there is allowed, and why the guide treats each of these places as a hazard.

Start with the street itself. On a one-way street, you may usually park on either the left side or the right side, because all traffic flows the same way. A two-way street is different. You must not park on the left side of a two-way street, and you must never park with your vehicle facing against the flow of traffic. A car parked on the left of a two-way street ends up facing oncoming traffic, which creates a hazard when it pulls in or out. So the street type comes first: one-way streets usually allow both sides, two-way streets only the right.

lines.text: Signs may ban or limit parking.
Colored curbs can do the same.

narration.text: Next, read the signs and the curb. The guide tells you to look for signs that ban or limit parking, and to notice that some limits are shown by colored curb markings instead of signs. A painted curb can carry a rule even where no sign is posted. The clearest example is a curb painted yellow, which means no parking there. So when you pull up to a curb, look at two things: the posts for any parking signs, and the paint on the curb itself. Either one can tell you that this spot is not available, or that parking there is limited.

title.text: Places that are always off limits

narration.text: Some places are banned no matter what the signs say. Never park inside an intersection, on a crosswalk, on a sidewalk, or across the entrance to a driveway. These spots block people walking, block other drivers turning, or trap someone in their own driveway. Parking is also forbidden next to a curb painted yellow, on a bridge, and in front of a fire hydrant, where emergency crews need clear access. Group them in your mind: places where people cross or walk, places where cars enter or turn, and places that must stay clear for safety, such as bridges and hydrants.

title.text: No sign does not mean yes

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers assume that if there is no sign, parking must be fine. The guide says otherwise. Colored curb markings can signal a parking limit even where no sign is posted, and a curb painted yellow means you may not park there. The same thinking applies to the always-banned places: you will not find a sign at every crosswalk or driveway telling you not to park, yet parking there is still forbidden. On a test, if a scenario mentions a yellow curb with no sign, the answer is still no parking. The paint is the rule.

Here is a quick check: you are driving on a two-way street and see an empty spot on the left side, just ahead of you. May you pull across and park there? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. On a two-way street you must not park on the left side, and you must not park facing against the flow of traffic, which is exactly what that spot would require. If the street were one-way, the left side would usually be allowed, because a one-way street usually lets you park on either side. The street type decides the answer.

lines.text: Then signs, paint and banned spots.

narration.text: To wrap up, here is a simple order for deciding whether a spot is legal. First, check the street type: one-way streets usually allow either side, two-way streets never the left, and never park facing traffic. Second, read the signs and the curb paint, remembering that a yellow curb means no parking even without a sign. Third, make sure you are not in an intersection, on a crosswalk or sidewalk, across a driveway entrance, on a bridge or in front of a fire hydrant. Next, you will learn the special rules for handicapped parking spaces and the fines that apply.

why_how.text: Reserved spaces only work for people with disabilities if other drivers leave them, and their access aisles, open.
Missouri backs these rules with a fine for misusing a reserved space.

scenario.text: Dev borrows his father's car, which carries a disability placard, and drives to the store alone.

reasoning.text: His father is not in the car, so the placard does not allow Dev to use a reserved space.

result.text: Dev parks in a regular space instead.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a displayed placard alone makes it legal to use a reserved space.

correction.text: The space also needs a person with a physical disability in the car or being dropped off or picked up.

memory_support.text: Placard plus the person, and keep the stripes empty.

prompt.text: Your car shows a placard, but the placard holder is at home. May you use the reserved space?

answer.text: No. The person with the disability must be riding along or being dropped off or picked up.

rationale.text: A placard alone is not enough, and using someone's placard when that person is not along is illegal.

lines.text: Who may use them, and when.
The aisle, the placard and the fine.

narration.text: This lesson covers handicapped parking. Reserved spaces exist so that people with disabilities can reach buildings safely, and the rules around them are strict. You will learn what the International Symbol of Access marks, which vehicles may use a reserved space and exactly when, why the striped access aisle next to the space must stay empty, why using someone else's placard can be illegal, and what fine a conviction can bring. Pay close attention to the condition that a person with a disability must be present, because that is the part most often misunderstood.

lines.text: A placard or plates must show.
A person with a disability must be present.

narration.text: The International Symbol of Access marks spaces reserved for vehicles driven by or carrying people with disabilities. A handicapped space may be used only by a vehicle that shows a disability placard or disability plates, and only while a person with a physical disability is in the vehicle or is being dropped off or picked up. Both conditions matter. The placard or plates identify the vehicle, and the person's presence is what makes using the space legal at that moment. If either one is missing, the space is not yours to use, even for a short stop.

Here is the trap that catches many drivers. They see a placard hanging from the mirror and assume the car may park in any reserved space. The guide says that showing a placard or plates is not enough by itself. The reserved space also needs a person with a physical disability riding in the car, or being dropped off or picked up right there. So a family member running an errand alone in a car with a placard may not use the space. On a test, look for whether the person with the disability is actually present. If not, the answer is no.

lines.text: Never park in the striped aisle.
Never use a placard without its holder.

narration.text: Two more rules protect reserved spaces. First, parking in the striped access aisle beside a handicapped space is illegal. That aisle gives room for wheelchairs, ramps and doors to open fully, so it must stay empty even though it looks like spare pavement. Second, using someone else's disability placard or plates to take a handicapped space is illegal when that person is not riding along at the time. The guide treats these as two separate offenses: one is about where you park, the aisle, and the other is about whose placard you use and whether that person is with you.

lines.text: No more than three hundred dollars.

narration.text: Missouri enforces these rules with a fine. A conviction for misusing a handicapped space brings a fine of at least fifty dollars and no more than three hundred dollars. Remember the two ends of the range: fifty at the low end and three hundred at the high end. Misuse includes parking in a reserved space without meeting both conditions, so a car with no placard, or a car with a placard but no person with a disability along, can both lead to that fine. The money is a reminder that these spaces are not a convenience for everyone, but a protected need.

Here is a quick check: you are driving your aunt's car, which has a disability placard, and you stop at the pharmacy by yourself while she stays at home. May you use the reserved space by the door? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. A placard alone does not make the space available. A person with a physical disability must be in the car or being dropped off or picked up, and using someone's placard when that person is not riding along is illegal. Park in a regular space, and leave the striped aisle empty too.

lines.text: Aisle empty, fifty to three hundred dollars.

narration.text: Let us sum up. The International Symbol of Access marks reserved spaces. You may use one only when your vehicle shows a disability placard or plates and a person with a physical disability is in it or is being dropped off or picked up. Never park in the striped access aisle, and never use another person's placard when that person is not with you; those are two separate offenses. A conviction for misusing a reserved space brings a fine of fifty to three hundred dollars. Next, you will learn how to park on a hill so the car cannot roll into traffic.

why_how.text: A car parked on a hill can roll if the brake slips, so the wheels must send it away from traffic.
The hill checklist makes sure the engine, gear, brake, keys and locks are all handled.

scenario.text: Lena parks facing downhill on a steep street and is about to get out.

reasoning.text: She turns the wheels sharply toward the side of the road, shuts off the engine in gear, and sets the parking brake.

result.text: She takes the keys, checks the mirror, steps out and locks the car.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking the emergency brake on the hill checklist is a different brake from the parking brake.

correction.text: The checklist uses emergency or parking brake for the same brake that is set on any parked vehicle.

memory_support.text: On a hill, wheels to the side, so it rolls away from traffic.

prompt.text: Why do you turn the wheels toward the side of the road when you park on a hill?

answer.text: So the car rolls away from traffic if it starts to move.

rationale.text: Turning the wheels sharply toward the roadside sends a rolling car away from moving traffic.

narration.text: Parking on a hill adds one big risk: the car can roll. This lesson teaches the steps that keep a parked car from rolling into traffic. You will learn which way to turn the front wheels and the reason behind it, then the checklist the guide gives for leaving a car on a hill, from the wheels and the engine to the brake, the keys, the mirror and the locks. You will also clear up one point of wording that confuses some learners, the emergency brake. By the end you should be able to list the hill steps in order and explain why each one is there.

lines.text: Point them toward the side of the road.
A rolling car moves away from traffic.

narration.text: When you park on a hill, turn the front wheels sharply toward the side of the road. The guide gives the reason directly: if the car starts to roll, the turned wheels steer it away from traffic instead of into the lane. Think of the wheels as your backup plan. The brake and the gear are supposed to hold the car, but if something slips, the wheels make sure the car heads for the roadside, not into passing vehicles. A slight turn is not enough; the guide says sharply, so the car would turn off the road quickly if it moved.

lines.text: Turn the wheels the proper way.
Shut off the engine in the proper gear.
Set the parking or emergency brake.

narration.text: The guide lists the first steps before you leave a car parked on a hill. Turn the wheels the proper way, toward the side of the road. Shut off the engine with the vehicle in the proper gear, which ties back to the earlier rule of gear for a manual and park for an automatic. Then set the parking or emergency brake. Each step adds a layer of protection: the brake holds the car, the gear backs up the brake, and the wheels decide where the car goes if both fail. Follow them in order and the car stays put. Do not skip any of them.

lines.text: It is set on every parked car.

narration.text: Here is a small trap in the wording. The hill checklist says to set the parking or emergency brake. Some learners think this means a special emergency brake used only on hills, separate from the parking brake they set everywhere else. It does not. The guide uses the words emergency brake and parking brake for the same brake, the one that must be set on any parked vehicle. So there is nothing extra to find on a hill. You set the same brake you always set, and the hill steps add the wheel turn on top of your usual routine.

lines.text: Check the mirror before stepping out.
Lock up and keep the keys.

narration.text: The hill checklist finishes with security and safety as you leave. Take the keys out of the ignition. Before stepping out, check the rearview mirror for traffic, since you will be opening a door next to the lane. Then lock the car and keep the keys with you. Notice that this ending is the same habit you use at any other stop: key out, car locked, keys in your pocket. The only difference on a hill is the earlier wheel turn. So if you already have the everyday routine, the hill version is easy to remember. Never leave the keys in the car.

Here is a quick check: you have parked on a steep hill and turned your wheels sharply toward the side of the road. A friend asks why you bothered, since the brake is already set. What is the reason? Work it out before reading on. The answer is that if the car starts to move, the turned wheels make it roll away from traffic instead of into the lane. The brake and the gear are meant to hold the car, and the wheel turn is the backup. That is why the guide asks for the wheels to be turned sharply, not just a little. The wheels are the last line of defense.

To close, here is the full hill routine. Turn the wheels sharply toward the side of the road so a rolling car moves away from traffic. Shut off the engine with the car in the proper gear. Set the parking brake, which the checklist also calls the emergency brake. Take the keys out, check the rearview mirror before you step out, then lock the car and keep the keys with you. That last part is the same security habit you use at every stop. In the final lesson of this chapter, you will learn parallel parking step by step.

why_how.text: Parallel parking follows a fixed sequence, and doing the turns in the right order is what makes it work.
Ending in the middle of the space leaves room for the cars ahead and behind.

scenario.text: Omar finds an empty space along the curb between two parked cars.

reasoning.text: He stops beside the car in front of the space, backs in with the wheels sharp right, swings sharp left once his front clears, then sharp right toward the curb.

result.text: He ends centered in the space.

claim.text: Common mistake: starting the backing turn with the wheels sharp left.

correction.text: The turns run sharp right, then sharp left, then sharp right again.

prompt.text: You are backing into a parallel space and your front end has just cleared the car ahead. Which way do the wheels go now?

answer.text: Sharply left while you keep backing.

rationale.text: After the first sharp right, the wheels go sharp left once the front clears, then sharp right as you pull toward the curb.

narration.text: Parallel parking is the skill many new drivers worry about most, but the guide breaks it into a short, fixed sequence. In this lesson you will learn where to stop before you begin, how to back into the space with the wheels turned sharply right, when to switch to a sharp left, and how to finish with a sharp right as you pull toward the curb. You will also learn where the car should end up. The key to the whole maneuver is the order of the wheel turns, so listen for right, left and right as we go through each step together.

lines.text: Stop beside the car ahead of the space.
Leave about one and a half feet.

narration.text: Everything starts with the right position. Pull up and stop alongside the car that is parked in front of the empty space, about one and a half feet to its left. Being beside that car, not behind the space, gives you the angle you need to back in. Being about one and a half feet away gives you enough room to swing in without scraping the other car, while staying close enough to reach the space. Before you move, remember to check traffic around you, since the next step means backing up and swinging the front of your car slightly toward the lane.

lines.text: Front clears the car ahead: sharp left.
Then sharp right and pull forward.

narration.text: Once your front end clears the car ahead, turn the wheels sharply left and keep backing. This straightens the car and brings the front in toward the curb. Then turn the wheels sharply right again and pull forward toward the curb, so the car settles in line with the others. Your goal is to end in the middle of the space, not pressed against the car ahead or the car behind. Leaving room on both ends lets those drivers pull out later. If you end up too close to one car, a small adjustment forward or back fixes it. Take it slowly and keep checking around you.

lines.text: The first turn is sharp right.
The middle turn is sharp left.
The last turn is sharp right.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Under pressure, many drivers start with the wrong turn or forget the last one. The guide's order is fixed: sharp right as you back into the space, sharp left once your front clears the car ahead, then sharp right again as you pull forward toward the curb. If a question offers left, right, left, or right, right, left, it has the order wrong. Saying the order to yourself while you practice helps it become automatic: right, left, right. Then finish centered in the space, with room on both ends for the cars around you.

Here is a quick check: you are backing into a parallel space. You started beside the car ahead and backed in with the wheels sharp right, and your front end has just cleared the car ahead. Which way do you turn the wheels now? Work it out before reading on. The answer is sharp left while you keep backing. After that, you turn sharp right and pull forward toward the curb, so the full order is right, left, right. If you said right again, that is the last turn of the sequence, which comes only after the sharp left has straightened the car.

Let us finish the chapter with the full parallel parking sequence. Stop beside the car in front of the empty space, about one and a half feet to its left. Turn the wheels sharply right and back slowly in, keeping your front end out of traffic. When your front clears the car ahead, turn sharply left and keep backing. Then turn sharply right and pull forward toward the curb, ending in the middle of the space. Remember the order, right, left, right, and finish with the parking routine you learned earlier: brake, gear or park, keys and locks.
